newsitem.title: USA: BEFORE THE BELL - Intel hits new high.
newsitem.headline: BEFORE THE BELL - Intel hits new high.

text.p: Shares in Intel Corp soared to a new all-time high preceding Tuesday's U.S. market open on the company's announcement last night that third quarter revenues will be better than earlier forecasts.
Ahead of the market open, shares in the semiconductor giant traded at 93-1/8, then rose as high as 94, up from yesterday's 88-5/8 close, according to Instinet.
Intel said it expects third quarter revenues to grow five percent or more from second quarter revenues of $4.62 billion.
Also, Intel said its "turns," or orders for immediate delivery, appear to be better than originally expected.
Previously, Intel was expecting third quarter revenues to be flat with the prior period and gross margins to be at the upper end of the model of 50 percent, plus or minus a couple of points, it said.
Now, Intel expects gross margins in the third quarter to be "above the 50 percent plus or minus a couple of points."
In last year's third quarter, Intel netted $931 million, or $1.05 per share, on sales of $4.17 billion, including $37 million pre-tax gain, or $0.03 per share after taxes.
The First Call consensus earnings for Intel's third quarter is $1.14 per share.
Intel will report third quarter earnings October 14, it said.
Tuesday's early stock gains added to the 3-3/8 rise to 92 in after-hours trade last night, traders said.
Further supporting the stock was Merrill Lynch raising its Intel earnings estimates this morning.
Merrill said it now expects the company to earn $4.65 to $4.70 per share this year, up from $4.50, and $6.20 per share in 1997, up from $5.80.
"Intel has got the whole group up," a trader said.
Before the open, Applied Materials Inc gained one to 26-3/4 and Lam Research rose 1-1/4 to 26.

Outside the technology stocks, Philip Morris Cos Inc jumped 2-1/8 to 94-1/8 after the company said a Florida circuit judge dismissed all the pre-1994 claims in the Medicaid suit brought against the tobacco industry by the state of Florida.
The court ruled that a recent state Supreme Court decision held that those claims could not go forward under the 1994 Florida Medicaid Amendments, Philip Morris said.
